Triggers.value: People who look similar to the victims
When people say things like my ex

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred
become overly compliant when feeling threatened

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

vignette: Kavita, a 37-year-old South Asian woman married and the owner of a small shop in her neighborhood, has been struggling with intense symptoms following a sexual assault that occurred several months ago. The traumatic event left deep scars on both Kavita's mind and daily life, affecting how she perceives her surroundings and interacts with others. The assault happened one evening as Kavita was closing up her shop late. A man who had been lurking outside forced his way in and attacked her. Since then, any reminder of that fateful night triggers a wave of fear and anxiety for Kavita. The mere sound of someone saying things reminiscent of her ex-boyfriend or the sight of people resembling victims from other reported assaults sends shivers down her spine. These triggers not only cause immediate distress but also make her avoid public transport, as it brings back the same sense of vulnerability she felt during the assault. Kavita's avoidance behaviors are part of a larger pattern of maladaptive strategies she has adopted to cope with the trauma. She spends most of her days in isolation, fearing that any encounter could trigger another episode of intense fear and anxiety. Her inability to put the traumatic event into words exacerbates this cycle; she often finds herself overwhelmed by nonverbal memories that are as vivid as they were on the night of the assault. The flashbacks Kavita experiences further compound her distress. In those moments, she feels as if the assault is happening all over again, and even simple movements from others can put her on high alert. She often positions herself so that her back is against a wall where she can see everything around her—a strategy to feel safer in public spaces. Kavita's memory of the event brings intense guilt and terror. Every time she recalls it, she feels an overwhelming sense of shame and fear, which intensifies her threat perception. Her flashbacks are so vivid that they often lead her to relive the traumatic experience, making her even more vigilant about potential triggers in her environment. Her counterfactual thinking—pondering how life would have been different if the assault had not occurred—keeps her trapped in a cycle of regret and fear. This thinking exacerbates her guilt and further deepens her maladaptive strategies. She becomes overly compliant, often going along with others’ wishes to avoid any potential threat or conflict. Kavita’s occupation as a shopowner has also been affected by these symptoms. The constant need for vigilance makes it difficult for her to run the store without feeling on edge all the time. Her interactions with customers have become strained, and she often finds herself avoiding eye contact or stepping away when they move suddenly. The combination of triggers, maladaptive strategies, memory difficulties, and heightened threat perception has led Kavita into a vicious cycle where each component reinforces the others. She feels stuck in this loop and is beginning to realize that her daily life is becoming increasingly unbearable. The intensity of her symptoms and their impact on both her personal and professional life finally pushed Kavita to seek help. Kavita’s most significant fear is reliving the trauma, but she also harbors hope for a future where she can navigate through everyday life without constant dread. She hopes that with therapy, she can regain control over her thoughts and actions, allowing her to feel safe in public spaces once again and to reconnect with those around her.
